report.source_text: Intravenous methylprednisolone, 30 mg/kg/day over 3 days, and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), 2 g/kg over 2 days, were given for the MIS-C. This was followed by 2 mg/kg/day of oral prednisone that was gradually weaned over a 4-week period. The response to treatment was positive with improvements seen in blood pressure, ejection fraction and fall in inflammatory markers (C reactive protein, ferritin and erythrocyte sedimentation rate). Additional supportive treatment included low-dose molecular-weight heparin and low-dose aspirin (for coronary artery protection and antiplatelet cover to prevent risk of thromboembolic events associated with MIS-C), calcium, vitamin D and zinc supplementation.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 7-year-old girl presented with a 4-day history of fever, sore throat, cough, diarrhoea, headaches, bilateral non-suppurative conjunctivitis, erythematous desquamating rash, and swelling of hands and feet, consistent with Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C). She was in shock with hypotension and tachycardia. Initial laboratory investigations revealed leucocytosis, elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 292 mg/L, ferritin 1022 μg/L, D-dimer 11.65 mg/L), and markedly elevated cardiac enzymes (troponin T 477 ng/L, pro-BNP 98900 ng/L), with positive SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibodies and negative PCR. She was treated for MIS-C with intravenous methylprednisolone and IVIG, followed by oral prednisone, showing a positive response with improved blood pressure, ejection fraction, and falling inflammatory markers. Following discharge from the PICU, she developed myalgia and marked proximal muscle weakness, with an elevated creatine kinase (6617 u/L). Acetylcholine receptor antibody tested positive (0.51 nm/L). She was diagnosed with myasthenia gravis and treated with pyridostigmine, low-dose oral corticosteroids, and methotrexate, along with intensive physiotherapy. One month post-discharge, her ptosis had completely resolved, and there was marked improvement in proximal muscle weakness, leading to the slow discontinuation of pyridostigmine and corticosteroids, indicating a transient course.
